title: Suppression: consciously setting aside distress (mature defense)
vignette: A medical student just finished the USMLE Step 1 examination and is anxious about her performance. She is especially unnerved when fellow students talk about the difficulty of the examination and discuss their answers to certain questions. The student decides not to think about the examination until her score arrives because "worrying isn't going to change the result." She is delighted when she receives a passing score several weeks later. Before receiving the result, the student exhibited which of the following defense mechanisms?

clues.text: decides not to think about the examination until her score arrives
clues.note: A CONSCIOUS choice to set aside distressing thoughts until a better time is SUPPRESSION - a mature defense mechanism.

clues.text: worrying isn't going to change the result
clues.note: She acknowledges her anxiety but deliberately (consciously) chooses not to dwell on it - the hallmark of suppression (vs repression, which is unconscious).

whatMatters: Consciously choosing to put aside distressing thoughts/feelings to cope with the present ('I won't think about it until the score comes') is SUPPRESSION - a MATURE defense mechanism. Answer F. (It differs from REPRESSION, which is UNCONSCIOUS blocking of thoughts.)
strategy: Key distinction: suppression is CONSCIOUS/deliberate; repression is UNCONSCIOUS. She is aware of her anxiety but deliberately defers it -> suppression. Reject repression (unconscious), rationalization (making excuses/justifying), displacement (redirecting feelings onto another target), intellectualization (focusing on abstract/nonemotional details), and isolation of affect (separating emotion from the event).

eliminations.label: Displacement - redirecting feelings onto another target
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: transferring feelings from the source onto a less threatening person/object (e.g., yelling at a spouse after a bad exam). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she isn't redirecting her anxiety onto anything - she's deliberately setting it aside. ✅ Correct if: taking out anger on an unrelated target.

eliminations.label: Intellectualization - focusing on abstract details
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: dwelling on nonemotional, abstract facts to avoid feelings (e.g., obsessing over pass-rate statistics). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she is not analyzing details; she is choosing not to think about it at all. ✅ Correct if: excessive abstract reasoning to avoid emotion.

eliminations.label: Isolation of affect - separating emotion from the event
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: recalling a distressing event WITHOUT the associated feelings. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she still HAS the anxious feeling; she consciously defers dwelling on it (suppression), not stripping the emotion away. ✅ Correct if: describing a traumatic event with no emotional reaction.

eliminations.label: Rationalization - making excuses/justifying (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: justifying behavior/outcomes with plausible but false reasons (e.g., blaming a poor score on 'badly worded questions'). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she isn't excusing or justifying - she consciously chooses not to dwell on the anxiety. ✅ Correct if: creating self-serving justifications.

eliminations.label: Repression - UNCONSCIOUS blocking
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: involuntarily/UNCONSCIOUSLY keeping distressing thoughts out of awareness (e.g., an adult with no memory of childhood abuse). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: she is AWARE of her anxiety and makes a CONSCIOUS decision to defer it - that's suppression, not repression. ✅ Correct if: unconscious, involuntary forgetting of distress.

reasoning: She is aware of her anxiety but deliberately chooses not to dwell on it until the result arrives
Consciously setting aside distressing thoughts/feelings to cope with the present = suppression
Suppression is a MATURE defense mechanism (conscious), distinct from repression (unconscious)
mechanism: Defense mechanisms are unconscious (or, for suppression, conscious) strategies that protect against uncomfortable feelings. They range from IMMATURE/maladaptive (denial, acting out, projection, splitting, regression, displacement, rationalization, intellectualization, isolation of affect, reaction formation) to MATURE/adaptive (SUPPRESSION, sublimation, altruism, humor). SUPPRESSION is the CONSCIOUS, deliberate decision to put aside an unpleasant thought or feeling in order to cope with present reality - the person is AWARE of the discomfort but chooses not to attend to it right now (as this student does: 'I won't think about the exam until the score comes'). It is often confused with REPRESSION, in which distressing thoughts are kept out of conscious awareness UNCONSCIOUSLY and involuntarily (e.g., an adult who has no memory of childhood trauma). The key discriminator is conscious (suppression) versus unconscious (repression). The other options describe different mechanisms: displacement (redirecting feelings onto a safer target), intellectualization (retreating into abstract facts), isolation of affect (separating emotion from a memory), and rationalization (justifying with false reasons).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Psych > defense mechanisms: mature (suppression, sublimation, altruism, humor) vs immature; suppression = CONSCIOUS setting aside vs repression = UNCONSCIOUS blocking.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Conscious deferral of anxiety = suppression (mature), not repression (unconscious).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on suppression vs repression, mature vs immature defenses, isolation of affect, or rationalization? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Repression is UNCONSCIOUS; rationalization = excuses; displacement = redirect; intellectualization/isolation = detach emotion.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: suppression = conscious 'I'll deal with it later' (mature); repression = unconscious blocking.

memoryHook: Suppression is hitting the mental 'snooze' on purpose - she KNOWS she's anxious and chooses to deal with it later; repression would bury the anxiety without her ever knowing.
